Situation1: They send an occasional text to check in with their parents over the weekend.
Expectation2: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation2: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Story: It was already past midnight when my phone buzzed with a frantic call from Maya. Her voice trembled as she explained her car had broken down on the highway, and she was alone, scared, and needed me to come get her right away. I could hear the cars rushing by in the background, and I knew she had no one else to call. My heart raced as I grabbed my keys, but then I noticed a message from my mom, sent hours ago: “Just checking in, hope you’re safe. Love you.” I hadn’t replied all weekend, and I knew she worried when I didn’t respond. She always expected me to check in, especially late at night. I stood in the hallway, torn. If I left to help Maya, I’d be driving in the middle of the night without telling my parents, which would only make them worry more. But if I stopped to call or text my mom, I’d lose precious time getting to Maya, who was counting on me. My hands shook as I stared at my phone, feeling the weight of both expectations pressing down on me, unsure which role I should answer first.
